articles.headline: 3-Way Fight Shaping For Presidency
articles.author: By Ray Esch
articles.body:
Conrades, Maxwell, Ollendorff To Vie

Three juniors, George Conrades, Bob Maxwell and Frank Ollendorff, have entered the race for the student body presidency, one of four student body offices to be vied for in the coming campus elections.

Seven candidates have declared for three of the four offices and, with election day only 12 days away, there are no announced candidates for the vice-presidency. John Keltner, junior from Akron, O., was running unopposed for the senior class presidency at press time. His campaign is being managed by Robin Coffman.

Conrades, a member of Beta Theta Pi fraternity, from Poland, O., is being managed by Neil McPherson, while Maxwell, a Phi Delta Theta from Delaware, is being managed by Dean McCartney and Jack Winters. Frank Ollendorff is a member of Sigma Phi Epsilon from Cleveland, O. His campaign is being directed by Kurt Iverson and Jack Lavalle.

A two-way battle for the office of secretary is shaping up between sophomores Jan Logan, Delta Delta Delta from Beaver, Pa., and Pat Martin, Pi Beta Phi from Cincinnati, O. Miss Logan's campaign is under the direction of Nancy Snider and Mary Supler, while Miss Martin's campaign manager is Kay Galyean.

Treasurer Draws 2

Juniors Bruce Buchanan and Bob Zimmerman are in contention for the treasurership. Buchanan is a Delta Tau Delta from Hillsdale, Mich., and is being managed by Dave Rees.

Zimmerman, a member of Phi Gamma Delta fraternity from Akron, O., is being managed by Fred Manske.

articles.headline: AWS Vote Set Thursday
articles.body:
Misses Greenfield, Dunham Top Slate

Juniors Jan Dunham and Gwen Greenfield will run unopposed for the offices of executive president and judicial president, respectively, in tomorrow's AWS elections.

They were chosen by a student nominating committee and presented at Monday's AWS Chapel as candidates for the two top posts in the women's governmental organization.

Candidates for other AWS offices are as follows: executive secretary, Sigrid Lund, Wendy Morris and Nancy Newman; judicial secretary, Naomi Harrison, Christie Lichliter and Norma Jean Ott; treasurer, Di Crowgey and Carol Robinson.

Dorm Nominee Slated

Carol Ailes and Joyce Ford were nominated for Austin Hall president, Nancy Jenkins and Julie Smith for senior class representative, Pat Latin and Lois Oswald for Monnett president, Paula Hellriegel and Judy Peterka for junior class representative and Bonnie Butler, Anne Fauver, Sue McWilliams, Marilyn Milliff and Sunny Wheeler for sophomore class representative.

Social committee chairman nominees are Connie McNeil, Julie Martin, Sue Schumaker and Sally Soncha. Mary Lynn Kevolic and Julie Kirkpatrick are running for the office of publicity chairman, and Jan Klein and Nancy Rickey for the office of standards chairman.

Jan Allen is running unopposed for town representative.

Candidates Interviewed

Candidates were chosen after interviews with the nominating committee, composed of present AWS officers and representatives from each class. Other women were permitted to file petitions for candidacy Feb. 18-22.

articles.headline: 1960 Bijou Queen Pick Slated Greek Week End
articles.body:
The 1960 Le Bijou queen will be crowned at the annual Greek Week Ball, Mar. 19, from a court of six OWU coeds, Dennis Appleyard, yearbook editor, announced.

One representative from each sorority and an independent woman form the group of 13 candidates who will be interviewed by a board of five judges, composed of four Bijou editors and the Transcript editor.

The 13 candidates and their sponsoring groups are: Sue Bode, Alpha Chi Omega; Pat Huhn, Alpha Delta Pi; Phebe Horning, Alpha Xi Delta; Sue Dodge, Chi Omega; Marjorie Whiteneck, Gamma Phi Beta; Anita Garcia, Kappa Kappa Gamma; Jan Stillinger, Kappa Alpha Theta; Kay Galyean, Pi Beta Phi; Bobbie Habbe, Zeta Tau Alpha; Marilyn Lais, Delta Delta Delta; Marilyn Ellis, Delta Gamma, and Linda Johnson, Independent Women.

The court will be selected and announced at the intermission of the ball. The queen and two runners-up will be announced at the close of the dance, Appleyard said.

Candidates will be judged on their photogenic qualities, poise and beauty and college extra-curricular activities, according to Appleyard.

articles.headline: Greek Heads Will Hear Rush Plan
articles.body:
Committee Seeks Deferred Pledging

The Fraternity President's Assembly was to hear a deferred pledging program for fraternities tonight, according to Fred Manske, chairman of the IFC Rush Committee, which drew up the plan.

The proposal would divide rush week activities into three periods, with rush to begin on Saturday noon and pledging deferred until Tuesday evening.

During the first period, each rushee "will be required to visit 12 different fraternity houses," the proposal states. Bids could be extended during this period, but rushees would not be allowed to accept them until Wednesday morning.

Divide Into Groups

The plan would divide the rushees into alphabetical groups and send them through the first series of visits on a three or four-day timetable.

By 10 p.m. Tuesday night each fraternity would submit to IFC a list of rushees that they would like to see a second time, according to the proposal. These lists would be mimeographed and handed out to each 

rushee so that he could "make an intelligent selection of houses for return visits," the plan states.

Each rushee would be required to select from four to six houses for return visits during the second period of rush, which would extend from Wednesday morning until Thursday evening of rush week.

The rushees' selections would be collected Tuesday night and turned over to the rush chairmen through IFC.

A ticket system wherein each rush chairman would get a ticket for each rushee visit would supply the means of enforcing the plan, according to Manske.

After the rushee revisits the minimum of four houses during the second period, he "would be allowed to return to any house as long as he followed his schedule that he set up Tuesday night," the plan specifies.

Pledging Starts Wed.

Pledge pins could be accepted from Wednesday morning on, under the proposed system.

In addition, the plan prohibits transportation of rushees by fraternity men, rushing outside fraternity property and rushee-visits during unscheduled hours.

Violations of the rules by rushees would be punished by removing the offender from rush until the beginning of open rush on Friday of rush week, Manske said.

articles.headline: Artist Series Finale Offers Szell, Cleveland Symphony
articles.author: By Pat Hanna
articles.body:
Transcript Staff

"One of the very best in our country," Charles E. Thompson, associate professor of music, commented about the Cleveland Symphony Orchestra, which will present "The Song of Earth" by Gustav Mahler and "Symphony in E-Flat Major" by Mozart this Sunday at 8:15 p.m. in Gray Chapel.

The concert, the last of this year's Artist Series, is the third presentation of this program given by the orchestra. The others were performed in New York and Cleveland.

Of the New York performance, Howard Taubman, critic for the New York Times said: "George Szell and the Cleveland Orchestra gave a Carnegie Hall concert that qualifies as one of the season's memorable events."

Honors Composer's Birth

"The Song of Earth" is being performed by many orchestras throughout the country in honor of the 100th anniversary of the composer's birth.

Directing the concert will be Musical Director and Conductor George Szell, who is in his 14th year with the orchestra. Soloists will be Maureen Forrester, Canadian contralto, and Ernest Haefliger, tenor from the Berlin Opera.

The Cleveland Orchestra, now in its 42nd season, has traveled widely throughout the eastern half of the United States and has given concerts in Canada and Cuba. It made its first European tour in 1957.

1,698 Tour Concerts

Since its founding in 1918, the orchestra has played a total of 1,698 concerts on tour. This spring the orchestra will embark on its first tour to the principal cities of the western United States.

Miss Forrester is making a return performance, having given a recital on Feb. 5 in Gray Chapel, where she was warmly received. She is regarded as one of the most sought after and highly acclaimed young artists now appearing before the public.

Haefliger was first recognized for work in oratorio, particularly his interpretation of the evangelist in Bach's "Saint John's Passion."

articles.headline: IPP Will Stay; New Director Being Sought
articles.body:
The Ben Arneson Institute of Practical Politics will continue despite the pending resignation of Fred G. Burke, director of the Institute and associate professor of political science, according to George W. Burns, dean of the University.

Dean Burns announced last week that the Administration is "recruiting for applications for the position."

articles.headline: Council OK's Phone Plan Would Provide 12 More Dorm Phones
articles.body:
A plan providing for 12 additional phones in the women's dormitories was passed by Student Council Feb. 16.

The proposal will now be sent to the Administration for consideration, according to Student Government president Bryce Collier.

Cost of the equipment, according to the proposal, will be $1,194 including installation and rentals for the first year, and $630 rental each additional year.

The plan, submitted by OWU junior Lee Kettell, is an itemized version of his earlier proposal, which appeared in the Jan. 13 Transcript.

Additional provisions called for are eight phones and four "Hear-Here" boxes in the three women's dorms. (A "Hear-Here" box is a semi-enclosed booth housing a phone.)

Provisions include three additional phones in Monnett, three additional phones and two "Hear-Here" boxes in Austin and two additional phones and two "Hear-Here" boxes in Stuyvesant.

Locations of the phones and "Hear-Here" boxes in each dorm were decided upon by the degree of congestion at each existing dorm telephone, Kettell said.

In all locations cited by the proposal, 40 to 50 women now use a single phone.

articles.headline: Drill Team Places Third At Purdue
articles.body:
Ohio Wesleyan's AFROTC Cadet Drill Team placed third out of 17 entrants in the Purdue Invitational Drill Tournament held at Lafayette, Ind., last Saturday.

The OWU team, led by Commander Jack Lavalle, amassed a total of 412 points out of a possible 500, and was out-pointed only by first place Purdue and Loyola University of Chicago, Ill., which took second.

Ohio Wesleyan placed ahead of teams from such schools as Northwestern, Ohio State, Michigan State and the University of Illinois. This placement was the "first time the Ohio Wesleyan drill team has come close to placing in a meet of this size" said Lavalle.

In individual competition held Saturday morning, OWU's Karl Dixon placed fourth out of 110 competitors in a test of individual ability to follow drill orders. The OWU group, first to take the floor in the afternoon's team competition, was "astonished and happily surprised" when the judges' decisions were announced, said Lavalle.

Credit for the fine showing was attributed by Lavalle to "hard practice and outstanding team spirit."

Drill team plans for the future include a trip to the annual Cherry Blossom Festival in Washington D.C., Apr. 7-9, the OWU Military Ball, Mar. 5, and the Ohio State Invitational Drill Tournament in May.

articles.headline: Special Meeting To Talk Grades
articles.body:
The possibility of counting plusses and minuses in point averages will be discussed at a special Student Forum meeting this Sunday, Representative-at-Large Frank Dunbar announced at last Thursday's Forum meeting.

Academic Relations Committee Chairman Dick Hattwick presented his committee's findings on the plus and minus controversy to Student Council Feb. 16. At Dunbar's suggestion, Council decided to refer the matter to Forum to get a comprehensive view of student opinion.

Hattwick, speaking before Council, pointed out that the inclusion of plusses and minuses in figuring point averages would affect the class rank of many students.

Affects Class Rank

Class rank, he said, is included on each student's transcript of grades and is one of the principle factors taken into consideration for acceptance to graduate schools. Counting plusses and minuses, Hattwick commented, would make point averages more accurate, and therefore give greater accuracy to class rank.

The committee's findings also indicated that plusses and minuses could affect campus activities such as fraternity and sorority affiliation (going active), Dean's List, Phi Society, Phi Beta Kappa, ODK and other honoraries, sports eligibility and job prospects after graduation.

Several systems were shown which equate plusses and minuses to the present four-point grade scale. Council favored a system which would add a fraction of a point (approximately .25 to .33) to the number grade for each plus and subtract the same amount for each minus.

Balance Out, Hattwick Says

The basic argument against the inclusion of plusses and minuses, according to Hattwick, is that they balance out over a four year period, and therefore it is not worth the effort to the Registrar's Office and the Academic Relations Committee to take them into account.

After the special meeting Sunday Forum representatives will be asked to take the proposal back to their groups to determine student opinion on the issue.

articles.headline: Testing Policy Change Sought
articles.body:
An addition to the present University bluebook policy relating to tests following Homecoming and Monnett week ends will be presented to the faculty Academic Policy Committee later this month, according to Pat Henry, a member of the Student Government Academic Relations Committee.

The proposed addition states that "bluebooks shall be given on the Monday and Tuesday following Homecoming and Monnett week ends only with a majority vote approval of the classes in which the bluebooks are to be given. A bluebook can be given any other time that week in lieu of the regular bluebook schedule."

The suggested change was prompted by a campus-wide survey following Homecoming Week End this year.

The survey revealed that many conflicts arise from a desire "to serve the University" in the area of public relations by participating in the week end activities, while at the same time maintaining intense academic studies in preparation for a Monday or Tuesday bluebook, Miss Henry said.

articles.headline: Pi Sigma Alpha Inducts Seven
articles.body:
Two juniors and five seniors were initiated into Pi Sigma Alpha, political science honor society, last Sunday.

New members are Clayton Atwater, Karen Draut, Bob Hardgrove, Dick Hodge, Sue Hoehn, Sue McCabe and Marleah Sanders.

New Political Science Department Chairman Robert E. Lorish was named adviser to the group. Earl Warner, professor of political science, has advised the honorary since 1952.

articles.headline: Board Invites Applications
articles.body:
Posts Open For 7 On Paper, Yearbook

Applications for a new director of photography post and six other paid Transcript and Bijou positions were opened by the Publications Board last week end.

Notices listing a Mar. 1 deadline have been posted on the Transcript, Bijou and Journalism Office doors.

The positions and yearly salaries include three on the Transcript: editor, $350; managing editor, $300, and business manager, $300. Yearbook posts include editor, $300; managing editor, $250, and business manager, $250.

All six salaries are subject to reduction in the event of financial difficulties, and all six officers are eligible to share in any extra profits.

The new photography position, carrying a $300 salary, was created by the Board in an effort to minimize conflicting and overlapping efforts of two different photography staffs, particularly in use of the two Pfeiffer Natatorium darkrooms. Creation of the post eliminates one of the former Bijou managing editorships.

After applications for the seven positions have been circulated among the 14 Board members, applicants will be interviewed Mar. 11 and 12, and selections will be announced in the Mar. 16 Transcript.

The new Transcript staff heads will work with the current officers on two issues and then take over for the Apr. 6 issue. The 1961 Bijou officers will begin working immediately on plans for their edition of the yearbook.

In other action, the Board approved an expenditure of $70 from the Joint Sinking Fund for a more powerful Strobe-flash unit for Transcript photographers and $25 for replacement of the Transcript enlarger lens.

articles.headline: Faculty Series Presents Hladky
articles.body:
Cellist Robert Hladky, associate professor of music, will present a recital tomorrow night at 8:15 p. m. for the Faculty Music Series. It will be held in Sanborn Hall Auditorium.

Prof. Hladky will play "Divertimente" by Haydn, "Sonata in C Major, Opus 102" by Beethoven, "Sonata" by Shostakovich, "Kol Nidrei" by Bruch and "Rumanian Folk Dances" by Bartok.

Hladky is first cellist with the Columbus Symphony Orchestra and a member of the Ohio Wesleyan Duvall Trio. He has performed with orchestras in Rochester N.Y. and Oklahoma City, Okla. Hladky, who has spent eight years at Ohio Wesleyan, is a graduate of the Eastman School of Misic in Rochestra, N.Y., where he received his doctorate last year.

articles.headline: Comprehensive Exam Trial Badly Planned
articles.body:
Comprehensive examinations, at least on a trial basis, are now upon us. Presumably, the results of this year's senior all-major exams are to help determine the future of such a plan at Ohio Wesleyan.

LAST SPRING we questioned the validity and usefulness of such a trial, since the students would not have time nor advice with which to prepare for the exams. Some problems have, indeed, been ironed out since then, notably the question of what to do with inter-departmental majors (composite tests have been or are being drawn up).

Nevertheless, our basic doubts of this type of trial seem to be borne out in practice. We know of students who had changed majors this year but still were required to take the comprehensives covering their previous major field. This is justifiable, but several of these students received less than a week's advance warning that they would have to take the tests.

SINCE THE GRADES on this year's tests won't count in many cases, the students involved usually didn't study for them, or at least did not bother to undertake any extensive review. This isn't a criticism, however, since the exams have been worked into the students' regular schedules, with no review time allocated.

Denison University, on the other hand, gives its seniors at least a week off from classes to review for the tests. This, we hope, will be the case at OWU, if and when comprehensives are instituted on a regular basis.

The danger in this spring's ill-prepared trial run of the exams, however, lies in the probable nature of the results. Scores will be low, we predict, indicating a lack of correlation between various aspects of the students' major fields. But the kind of results needed for a valid test would stem from a trial program like the one now in use at Denison.

We condemn this year's test plan as an almost useless waste of time, both for the students involved and for the professors who must make up the exams and grade them. We hope that the expected low scores, if such turns out to be the case, will serve to emphasize the need for a class-free review period and advance warning of at least two years. It would be unfortunate if poor results this year should cloud the valid evaluation of such a potentially-desirable program as senior comprehensives.

articles.headline: Possible Honor System Involves Many Factors
articles.body:
A revival of interest in an honor system for Ohio Wesleyan is now apparent on campus, at least in Student Government, Trustee and Administration circles. Student Council has appointed a temporary committee to investigate the feasibility of setting up such a system at OWU.

THERE HAVE BEEN honor systems at OWU in the past, none of which has lasted into our time. Whether or not these earlier systems worked all right is not relevant, for we must consider the type of intellectual climate, or lack of it, which exists today.

We must agree that the objectives of an honor system are above reproach. Certainly encouragement of personal maturity and integrity in scholastic matters is a desirable end. And perhaps a minority of students would respond favorably to the institution of an honor system. But there are certain basic problems which we hope the SG committee will thoroughly investigate before making its report.

RIGHT NOW, IT SEEMS to us there is an obsessive emphasis upon grades at Ohio Wesleyan. This obsession stems only partially from the faculty and Administration's position. Students themselves use grade-points as a measuring stick for themselves and their fellows. Certain categories of students have this demand for high grades forced upon them, by the increasing competition for places in graduate schools. The interfraternity and intersorority house grade listings are avidly read each semester.

As long as the pressure for good grades dominates the OWU academic scene, the chances for a successful honor system would be in doubt. Social pressure, upon which most high school honor systems depends, may here be stronger or weaker regarding this matter. This factor should be examined.

In addition, the "right or wrong" of fraternity and sorority files systems should be taken into account when the report is draw up.

THERE ARE, OF COURSE, many other factors which must be taken into account before any recommendations, pro or con, can be made. We laud Council's action in investigating this area, for even if an honor system is found to be unfeasible at this time...

articles.headline: Hits Reviewing
articles.author: By Diser
articles.body:
Editor, the Transcript:

A university needs a student-run paper. It is necessary because without one we students wouldn't know how to think. But after we read your fascinating editorials and news columns, we do back the Bishops, pass the social fee, read the OWL receipts, smoke Philip Morris's, tote that barge etc.

That is, in almost all cases. But we cannot rely on you in one aspect—reviewing.

After we have seen a movie or a play, all conversation ceases while we await Wednesday and the review in the Transcript. But when Wednesday comes, do you tell us clearly and distinctly, in a fair but honest manner, what we are to think about the movie or play? No!

"Parroting" Hit

One reviewer is a parrot, repeating to her eager readers the publicity sent with the film, while the other, with his deep attachment to paired adjectives, praises everything in sight. This latter person demonstrates any. Let us be specific.

Joel Feldstein, the better of the two writers, wrote a fairly long review of "The Male Animal." Joel spent about half of his review summarizing the action of the play, which perhaps could have been made more vital by weaving it into the more important criticism, but which was done satisfactorily.

Quotes Remarks

The critical remarks showed that Catellone had "sensitivity, skill, and . . maturity"; Miss Parker had "grace and skill;" "Forsythe was "skillful and dignified"; Art Lord was "sufficiently inebriated"; Powers was "real and impressive"; and that "congratulations and praise goes (sic.)" to everyone.

I'm glad to hear that our Freshmen had such a flawless and believable show. I, for one, am not convinced.

"Glaring Flaw"

I will concede that Cartellone was good and that most of the cast was adequate, although not as good as Feldstein indicates. The most glaring flaw was his straight-faced comment that "Lord made his secondary role the highlight of the play and one of the most memorable roles."

While this statement seems to indicate that Lord was the best actor, a little thought will show that what is meant is that, in the important Drunk scene, Lord stole the show from Cartellone.

Lord performed an excellent solo nightclub act, but unfortunately (for Cartellone and the play, he had a "secondary role."

Good Ones Hard To Find?

I suppose it is hard to find a competent, unbiased review—alone in errors of judgments, however.

Mr. Judd, who reviewed "Antigone," had one member of the cast in a class. His praise for this student was not supported by most of my acquaintances.

Your other reviewer is Carol Luce, who is found on the last page with the headline " 'Felix Krull' Delightful." A reader of the review soon discovers that this is Miss Luce's only critical judgment upon the film.

Book Gets The Praise

The source, a book, receives high praise—"rollicking" and "wonderfully humorous." She also quotes several opinions 



from unspecified sources about how wonderful the acting is in the picture.

Perhaps she does not realize that a review is supposedly concerned with what the reviewer thinks of the film, not the book and not what others think.

I think that, as leaders in campus taste and judgment, you should face up to this problem seriously. You should realize that uncritical criticism on a college campus probably indicates a fear of hurting some feelings and that it is your duty to provide us, the readers, with the correct opinions for the week.

Philip Diser

articles.headline: Informal Benefits Of Meeting Hailed
articles.author: By Jerry Sell
articles.body:
The evaluation of the Five-College Conference held here last week end holds out little hope for the future of the organization. In reality it was a three-college conference, since only Oberlin, Ohio Wesleyan and Antioch sent delegates.

Then, too, many of the delegates felt that the discussion groups which attempted to share the schools' experiences in areas such as student government were only partially successful, at best.

All this may be true, but I would like to offer my own personal evaluation, which is that the Five-College Conference held here last week end was one of the most worthwhile events to happen on our campus this year.

Discussions Irrelevant

True, the discussion groups were probably of little benefit, as far as problem-solving is concerned. But that fact is irrelevant.

The value of such a conference lies in an area entirely apart from the formal programs. We'll all agree that no American Legionnaire goes to that group's national convention solely for the "business meeting." The conference here served a very valuable purpose far apart from the events listed on the printed program.

In the first place, all college students enjoy getting together with people from other schools. There seems to be a feeling of common tribulation among students which makes them love to congregate.

Lives Are Parochial

But, in addition, let's remember that we all live a fairly parochial and limited life at our colleges, associating largely with people who are quite alike and who have similar ideas.

I, for one, found it very enjoyable to talk to Oberlin students with ideas different from the ones prevalent here. I think, too, the Oberlin men present "enjoyed" meeting some OWU women, who, from accounts heard, were a different type than Oberlin's coeds.

Talks Are Invaluable

Some type of continuing conference among the many liberal arts colleges in Ohio is invaluable for the mutual education and recreation of all.

Mainly, the fact is that we all had a very good time, we all had some new experiences and all met some new people. What more reason does an institution need to justify its existence?

articles.headline: Test Explained
articles.body:
Editor, the Transcript:

For the benefit of those who have expressed a negative attitude toward the ethos questionnaires which have been circulating around campus since February 16, this public statement has been prepared 1) to answer general objections to the survey, 2) to explain more fully the methods and purposes of the survey, and 3) to suggest probable effects of the survey on Ohio Wesleyan University.

Most of the objections to the survey in general seem to be aimed at specific items which probe into moral attitude and behavior.

Little Research Done

The probable reason for this is well understood when we consider that little organized research has traditionally been conducted on moral behavior. As has happened in the case of all other educational and scientific advances that have been made throughout history, there is an almost natural tendency at first to eye with suspicion or hostility anything that is new, uncertain, unfamiliar, "strange," or "opposed to tradition." The resolution is simply a matter of becoming accustomed to and accepting new ideas in new areas of inquiry.

The questions used on our survey were submitted by students and faculty members who were interested in the sampling of campus opinion on the items they submitted.

On Requested Areas

The items, therefore, as a whole reflect those areas of greatest interest to both students and faculty on campus. The questions on the ethos survey are intended to sample more than the ordinary, outwardly expressible ("overt") attitudes that are commonly sampled in verbal surveys.

The questions on our survey will sample, moreover, the inner "hidden" ("covert") attitudes of human beings, hypothesized to be more influential than the "overt" attitudes in the determination of behavior.

Measure Attitude

We may assume that by measuring the kind of attitudes an individual reveals, we will have some idea of the kind of personality behavior he expresses.

On a sociological level, the "modal personality" of a number of persons in a group or subculture is known as the "ethos," or "basic personality" of the group: hence, the name of our survey.

We are attempting to characterize the "basic personality" pattern of Ohio Wesleyan University as a whole, as well as that of the principle subgroups within the university.

To Show Degree

A subjective interpretation of the statistics to be obtained on the morality questions simply will show the degree to which we are morally strong or morally weak; it will also point out the particular areas in which we need to develop greater moral strength or to alter our moral attitudes in order to behave in greater accordance with the moral laws of our society and of our faith.

Above all we should realize that at the present time we have no scientifically objectified basis for the "smug" attitude we now have toward our moral behavior, nor will we have any such rational basis until we began to get a favorable impression of ourselves from such quantitative and qualitative instruments as the all-campus ethos survey.

Will Aid Profs

Besides usefulness in studying at the sociological level the community in which we live, the ethos survey is expected to have much usefulness in helping deans, faculty members, resident counselors, and others who counsel individual students to analyze more accurately individual attitudes and behavior patterns by comparing them with those of the group and the campus.

Two necessary steps toward achieving our goal must first of all be realized, however: first, an understanding and an appreciation of the purpose of the study; and second, an acceptance of the need for the distribution of the survey questionnaire!

Given the necessary understanding, acceptance, and appreciation described above, we are confident that we shall succeed in making one of the most significant student contributions that Ohio Wesleyan has known in many year.

Lee Doering,
Chmn. Ethos Test Sub-Committee,
SG Academic Relations Committee

articles.headline: THREE WHO PASSED IN THE NIGHT
articles.author: By Max Shulman
articles.body:
Last year, as everyone knows, 1,210,614 undergraduates dropped out of college. 256,080 flunked; 309,656 got married; 375,621 ran out of money; and 309,254 found jobs. As you have, of course, observed, this accounts for only 1,210,611 out of 1,210,614. What happened to the other three?

Well sir, to find the answer, I recently completed a tour of American campuses where I interviewed 40 million students and sold several subscriptions to The Open Road for Boys, and it pleases me to report that I can now account for those three elusive undergraduates.

The first was an LSU junior named Fred Gaugin. He was extremely popular, always ready with a smile, fond of folk dancing and pralines, and last semester his Chi Psi brothers unanimously elected him treasurer of the fraternity. This proved an error. Gaugin, alas, promptly absconded with the money and went to Tahiti to paint. The fraternity is bending every effort to extradite Gaugin, but Tahiti, alas, is currently observing the feast of Dipthong, the Sun-God, a five-year ceremony during which all the islanders wear masks, so nobody, alas, can say for certain which one is Gaugin.

The second missing undergraduate is William Cullen Sigafoos, Oregon State freshman, who went one day last fall to a disreputable vendor named A. M. Sashweight to buy a pack of Marlboros. Mr. Sashweight did not have any Marlboros because Marlboros are only sold by reputable vendors. However, he told Sigafoos that he had another brand which was just as good, and Sigafoos, being but an innocent freshman, believed him.

Well sir, you and I know there is no other brand as good as Marlboros. That fine filter, that flavorful flavor, that pleasure, that joy, that fulfillment—are Marlboro's and Marlboro's alone. All of this was quickly apparent to young Sigafoos and he flew into a terrible rage. "As good as Marlboros indeed!" he shrieked, kicking his roommate furiously. "I am going right back to that mendacious Mr. Sashweight and give him a thrashing he won't soon forget!" With that he seized his lacrosse bat and rushed out.

Mr. Sashweight heard him coming and started running. Now Mr. Sashweight, before he became a disreputable vendor, had taken numerous prizes as a cross-country runner, and he thought he would soon outdistance young Sigafoos. But he reckoned without Sigafoos's stick-to-itiveness. At last report the two of them had passed Cleveland. When they reach the Atlantic Seaboard, bad Mr. Sashweight will get his lumps from Sigafoos, you may be sure, and I, for one, am glad.

The third missing undergraduate, also named Sigafoos, is a Bennington sophomore named Celeste Sigafoos and, ironically, she never intended to leave college at all. She was merely going home for Christmas on the Natchez, Mobile, and Boise Railroad, and during the night, alas, her upper berth slammed shut on her. Being a Bennington girl, she naturally did not wish to make an unseemly outcry, so she just kept silent. The next morning, alas, the railroad went bankrupt, and Miss Sigafoos today is lying forgotten on a siding near Valparaiso, Indiana. Fortunately she has plenty of Marlboros with her.

* * * * *

And how about the rest of you? Do you have plenty of Marlboros? Or if you like mildness but you don't like filters, do you have plenty of Philip Morris? Or if you want a king-size filter cigarette that is even milder than Marlboro, do you have plenty of the new Alpine?

articles.headline: OWU Staff Policies to Be Altered
articles.body:
University employment positions formerly held by non-student personnel are being evaluated in hopes of effecting an increase in the number of student employment opportunities, University Controller Robert Meyer told the Transcript last week.

The resignations of five janitors this month have left some part-time jobs open for Ohio Wesleyan men. Since the resignations became effective, four students have been placed on a snow-removal crew around University Hall, Meyer stated.

Drawbacks to granting student jobs, said Meyer, often arise from conflicts between classes and work hours and from the inefficiency involved in filling one full-time job with several part-time workers.

"We can't fire people," Meyer stressed, referring to present employees. "However, when vacancies that could be filled by students arise in the present maintenance force, these jobs will be given to students," he stated.

articles.headline: OWU Hosts Ohio MSM
articles.body:
Approximately 250 delegates from 14 universities will arrive at OWU this week end for the annual Spring Conference of the Ohio Methodist Student Movement.

Tinker Green, out-going SCF officer, said the program will be the "most significant one of the year" for Methodist students. The theme of the three-day conference is "God's Call . . Our Response."

Key speakers scheduled are Harold Ehrensperget, associate professor of religion and the arts at the Boston University School of Theology; Ruth Harris, secretary of student work at the Board of Missions in New York; the Rev. Lance Webb, North Broadway Methodist Church, Columbus and Richard Gay, director of religious activities at OWU.

Other features of the week end are two dance dramas to be put on by a Kent State University group Saturday night.

The $6 cost of the week end includes meals, insurance and registration fee, Miss Green said. Interested students may register at the office of Religious Activities no later than tomorrow at 5 p. m.

articles.headline: OWU Entertains 45 5-College Delegates
articles.body:
Approximately 45 delegates from Oberlin and Antioch attended the winter week end of the Five College Conference held at Ohio Wesleyan last Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

Denison and Wooster did not attend because of campus conflicts, according to Jane Polley, OWU conference chairman.

The general consensus was that the conference was successful, despite the absence of two of the other colleges, she said.

Miss Polley called the conference a descriptive rather than an active conference, since the main achievement was that of better understanding, rather than definite action.

The delegates did decide, however, that the Five College Conference needs re-organization and a more definite statement of purposes and goals, she said.

The delegates expressed the opinion that future conferences should emphasize more discussions on important campus and international events and put less emphasis on social activities, such as dances, to entertain the delegates. However, they did enjoy these activities and the experience of living in the dorms and fraternity houses of another college, she said.

Frank Dunbar, one of the discussion leaders, said the conference was important in that it "stimulated interest in a community of ideas." He felt that the ideals of the Five College Conference are excellent, even though the structure needs improvement.

Future plans for the conference made last week-end include a music exchange at Denison, Mar. 26 and another conference, sponsored by Antioch sometime in the Spring, at Bar Hollow Camp in Ohio.

articles.headline: Stendhal's Novel Suffers From Movie Adaptation
articles.author: By Connie McNeil
articles.body:
In the Lecture-Movie Series showing of the French film version of Stendhal's novel "The Red and the Black" last Friday, the psychological realism of individual integrity and class distinction was almost obscured.

Concentrating on Julien Sorel's romantic adventures, the film inadequately showed Sorel's duel nature—a personality split between hatred for hypocrisy and the necessity to be a hyocrite to succeed in 19th century France. This conflict was symbolized by the title: the red stood for the army, which Sorel really desired to enter; the black represented the clergy which he did enter because a peasant could advance faster there.

The plot became so melodramatic in the movie that serious moments produced laughter from the audience. Sorel, a carpenter's son, seduces the wife of the mayor, M. de Renal, in whose home he lives as tutor.

After staying in a severe monastary, Sorel becomes secretary to M. de la Mole in Paris. There he has an affair with de la Mole's daughter until a poisonous letter from his former mistress turns the household against him. He then shoots Mme. de Renal out of revenge for spoiling his success.

The focal point of the story comes when he repents for his hypocrisy and dies happy, knowing that he became great by not compromising in order to live. However the many psychological innuendoes of the book were condensed in the film to occasional humorous thoughts flashed on the screen, so that the viewer who hadn't read the novel could hardly perceive its meaningful content.

Danielle Darrieux, the famous French actress, played Mme. de Renal with force and dignity. The handsome Gerard Phillipe portrayed Sorel as a reckless rascal, omitting his quality of rationality.

The movie was filmed in predominant tones of red and black, which intensified the total effect. However, technical devices and famous actors did not obliterate the injustice done to Stendhal's novel.

articles.headline: Two Replace Absent Profs
articles.body:
Fill Vacancies In French, Philosophy

Two faculty replacements have been named by the Administration to serve during the leaves of absence of R. Bradshaw Angell, associate professor of philosophy, and Clarence E. Ficken, professor of French.

Andrew G. Oldenquist, part-time visiting instructor in philosophy, replaces Prof. Angell, who has a semester's leave, and Henry L. Chabert, assistant professor of French, has replaced Prof. Ficken, who has a year and a half leave to conduct personnel research.

Prof. Oldenquist was graduated from Northwestern University in 1953 and received his M.A. from Brown University in 1955. He did graduate work at Middlebury College in Vermont and studied at Gottingen and Munich universities in Germany on a Fulbright grant from 1957-59.

Prof. Oldenquist is completing work toward his Ph.D. at Ohio State, where he holds a graduate teaching assistantship.

Prof. Chabert, a French citizen, worked with the United Nations in Geneva and New York from 1957-59 as a writer and translator and taught French to UN personnel.

He was graduated from the Ecole des Sciences Politiques in 1935 and received his L.L.B. from the Paris Law School in 1941. His M.A. was earned at the Sorbonne in 1943. Before his work with the UN, Prof. Chabert was a professor of English literature and language at the College de Rosen in Versailles.

No replacement will be sought for Glenn E. Milligan, former associate professor of education, who resigned his position Feb. 1 to work on a project in Columbus, according to George W. Burns, vice-president of the University.

articles.body:
Paintings by two Ohio Wesleyan University art professors are on display this month in one-man shows. Jarvis Stewart, professor of fine arts, narrated yesterday his 15 expressionist and abstract-expressionist paintings showing this month at Otterbein College.

articles.headline: Phys Ed Upheld
articles.body:
No request for a change in the physical education grading system will be made by Student Government as a result of Student Council action last Tuesday.

Council voted favorably on a recommendation from the Academic Relations Committee, which declared that no change should be sought at the present time.

According to the committee’s report, the physical education grades 1) motivate students to learn the skills better, 2) force students to attend class, 3) give prospective employers and graduate schools another measure of the student’s ability, 4) help keep athletes academically eligible and 5) “keep up the morale of the physical education instructors."

The committee also listed the reasons why the system should be changed: 1) It constituted “academic imperfection” in that few other high-ranking schools continue a grading system in physical education, 2) grades prevent some students from learning new skills for fears of a poor mark, 3) the grades in physical education keep some students from making a 4.0, 4) a survey made by the committee was reported to show that 50 percent of the men and 82 percent of the women were dissatisfied with the system and 5) the gym grades can hurt point-averages, although the report also stated that a maximum of .2 of a point could be affected by a physical education mark.

In an interview last Friday, Glenn Fraser, professor of physical education, commented, “Many graduate schools, as well as honoraries such as Phi Beta Kappa, do not figure in physical education grades.”

articles.headline: Yugoslav Governmental Structure Described
articles.author: By Roger Thaler
articles.body:
(In the sixth article on his summer in Yugoslavia, Delaware Community Ambassador Roger Thaler outlines the local and national governmental systems, particularly since the communist country broke close ties with Russia in 1953. Thaler, an OWU senior, lived with a Yugoslav family under the Experiment in International Living.—Ed.)

The city governments in Yugoslavia, while having some similarities to ours, are much different in most respects. The six republics in Yugoslavia, similar to our states, are divided into many districts (like our counties).

Each district is divided into several communes, which constitute their city governments. Each commune then has its own separate commissions. Typical commissions are those on education, culture and social security.

In theory and from a structural viewpoint, the basic and most important instrument of authority is the Federal National Assembly. It consists of two houses: the Federal Council and the Council of Producers.

Entrust To President

The executive functions of the state have been entrusted by the Federal Executive Council to the president of the Republic.

Josip Broz Tito was elected the first president of the Republic in 1953. He was elected for the second time on Jan. 29, 1954, and for a third term in 1958.

Before Yugoslavia's break with Russia in 1953, their government reflected the U.S.S.R.'s in many respects—extreme centralism, fake federalism, rubber-stamp parliaments, police terror, arbitrary justice, thought control and one party rule.

After the break with Russia there was a decentralization of administration. These and other alterations made the constitution of 1946 obsolete, and in January 1953, a new constitution was adopted.

Embodies Federal Principle

The new constitution embodied the principle (on paper at least) "that the central organs, be they republican or federal, should actually perform only those functions" which the local people's committees "are unable to perform."

The constitutional framers hoped to develop the initiative of the masses and to give the people the feeling of democratic participation in the running of the government.

During the post-war years the Communists used many devices for obtaining large majorities in the elections. Finally in Setpember, 1953, the government decided to pass a new electoral law which contains the following features:

New Features Added

1) Nomination by open meetings of voters, 2) use of printed paper ballots and 3) plural candidacies. However, in a majority of the elections the candidates are Communists or Communist-approved.

Since the people know that the Communist party is not going to permit itself to be voted out of power, they often look on elections as a farce.

Wesleyan conferred an honorary doctor of science degree to him in 1937. Prof. Sears returned to Ohio Wesleyan as commencement speaker for the class of 1956.

articles.headline: Bishops Knock Off Heidelberg, 88-73; Prepare For Otterbein In OC Tourney
articles.author: By Tom Grissom
articles.body:
Sports Editor

Ohio Wesleyan faces Otterbein at 8 p.m. Friday in the first basketball tournament in the Ohio Conference's long history.

The Bishops drew the Otters in the drawings, held last Sunday afternoon at Capital University. Wittenberg encounters Denison in the opener at 6 p.m. and Marietta takes on Capital in the last game of the action-packed event.

The tourney has been broken down into two divisions, with preliminary games coming at Columbus and Akron, and the finals at the latter next week end. Two teams will be sent from each divisional playoff.

At Capital, Wittenberg and Muskingum will be seeded, and in the north, Akron and Oberlin are the choice teams. If the Bishops get past Otterbein they will face the Wittenberg-Denison winner at 7:30 on Saturday night.

Pre-tourney favorite is Wittenberg, still unbeaten at press time in Ohio Conference competition. The Tigers boast standout big men in 6 ft. 7 in. Tony Wilcox and George Fisher and 6 ft. 4 in. Bert Price, plus two swift guards in Don Wolfe and Tony Vedova.

Muskingum and Capital will draw the most support, behind Wittenberg, for the two seedings. Muskingum has the better conference mark, 10-2, but Capital has been ever-improving and is currently riding on a eight-game winning streak.

However, the surprise team of the whole show may well be the Battling Bishops of Ohio Wesleyan, who are the most improved team in the OC and perhaps underrated by more formidable opponents.

The Bishops have now won eight out of their last eleven games and are 10-10 for the season. The Bishops have found added scoring and rebounding punch in junior Bert DuPont. With Tom Nims' ankle healed, the Red and Black will be at peak strength for the finale of the season.

Ken Lauterer is the only senior on the team and so will be playing in his last games for the Bishops. Alice McAllister, chairman of the Bishop Boosters, urged students to support the team by sitting in a block section at the game. The Bishops' bench will be on the south side of Alumni Gym, and a section will be held there for all OWU students.

Tickets are available in the Physical Education office all this week at $1 and at Capital before the game for $1.50.

The high flying Ohio Wesleyan Battling Bishops whipped the Student Princes from Heidelberg Saturday night, 88-73. Earlier in the week the Bishops were nosed out by Mount Union, 71-64.

Getting off to a slow start, the Bishops' attack was hampered by the frequent and dubious shrill of the official's whistle.

Unusual Call

Early in the game an example of the questionable officiating was seen. Ray Slabaugh took a jump shot and was fouled by No. 11, Tom Gibson. The referee mistakenly called the foul on No. 20 (Slabaugh) and gave Slabaugh a foul shot. This brought screams from the Heidelberg bench that there was no player wearing No. 20 for the Student Princes.

Not acknowledging his own mistaken identity of jerseys, the ref marched the length of the floor and gave Gibson a bonus shot, thus charging Slabaugh with a foul as he took his shot.

But the Bishops were undaunted by their new opponent and sped to an early 22-16 lead in the opening minutes. With Jerry Vaughn and Slabaugh plugging away at the net with their long arching jump shots, the quintet widened the gap to 41-33 at intermission.

In the second half, as the Bishops worked on their lead, one of the most unusual plays to occur at Edwards Gym took place.

Unusual Play Seen

After taking a time out, Heidelberg was given the ball under its own basket. Forgetting at which end of the court they were, the Tiffin guards brought the ball up the floor and into OWU territory. Realizing they were aiming at the wrong goal, guard Duane Warns wheeled around a headed for his own basket and sunk the ball in the net, to the amazement of the Bishop basketballers and fans. An unusual night of basketball indeed!

Seven In Double Figures

Seven Bishops scored in double figures. Tom Eibel and Slabaugh led OWU with 14 each, Bill Miller hit for 13, Vaughn for 11 and DuPont, Nims and Tom Swaim each had 10.

High scorers for the Student Princes were Warns and Gibson, tallying 17 and 16, respectively.

articles.headline: IPP Misses In Kennedy, Nixon Try
articles.body:
Richard M. Nixon and John F. Kennedy have been contacted but will be unable to speak at the Ohio Wesleyan Political Days scheduled for this spring, Fred G. Burke, director of the Institute of Practical Politics, revealed to the Transcript last week.

Prof. Burke, who contacted the political figures two months ago, stated that both Nixon and Kennedy "gave the idea much consideration," but found they could not attend "due to pre-arranged schedules."

Prof. Burke also announced that he has contacted another Democratic senator to replace Kennedy, but refused to give the name until he receives a definite reply. He is planning to contact another Republican figure soon, he said.

According to Burke, the Political Days will be held sometime in April, but no definite date can be scheduled until speakers are obtained.

Howard N. Maxwell, professor of physics, is heading an Ohio Wesleyan committee that will work with the representatives of 13 other liberal arts colleges in Ohio, Indiana and Michigan in establishing a cooperatively planned curriculum.

articles.headline: OC Lead Will Be Prize Of Kenyon Meet Today
articles.author: By Bob Moyers
articles.body:
The OWU splashers made it 10 straight dual meet victories last week by blasting Baldwin Wallace, 57-37, and Oberlin, 65-30. Evan with this impressive record, Coach Dick Gordin's record-breakers will probably be listed as underdogs against the Lords. Although Kenyon has been defeated by Bowling Green and Miami of Ohio this season, the Lords will be favored due to their six straight conference championships and their decisive victory in the Ohio Conference Relays.

However, Coach Gordin believes that his swimmers have a good chance to upset the Lords if the breaks happen to fall in the right direction. The affable coach had one word to say in regards to a Bishop victory. He said, "Possibly."

In his six years at Ohio Wesleyan, Coach Gordin has never defeated the overpowering Lords. In fact, it is believed that no OWU swimming team has ever posted a victory over its regal rivals.

The Gordinmen would like nothing better than to end the reign of the conference champs who have caused OWU to come out second best during the past six years. With a perfect record hanging in the balance, the conference champions will be crowned at OWU on Mar. 4 and 5.

Waterfield, indvidual medley, broke the Ohio Conference record for the 200-yard butterfly with a clocking of 2:22.8. This time also breaks the OWU pool record and is a new Ohio Wesleyan record for the event.

Wink Franklin also continued his record-breaking ways with a record time of 2:00.0 in the 220-yard freestyle and a clocking of 5:17.1 in the 440-yard freestyle. Both times bettered the OWU record for the events.

Robin Farran, newly selected Athlete of the Week, broke Jerry Dickey's OWU record in the 200-yard breaststroke with a time of 2:39.9.

The Bishops won nine out of 11 events in their decisive victory, which included the second straight win for freshman diver Steve Spicer, who scored 141.75 points, for his best effort of the season.

Against Baldwin-Wallace last Saturday [illegible] won the event.

Al Waterfield set an OWU mark in the 200-yard backstroke with a time of 2:29.0, and Franklin and Farran set records in their specialities. The records did not stand for long however, as both Franklin and Farran bettered their times in Saturday's meet.

articles.headline: Press Box
articles.author: By Rog Lockwood
articles.body:
After the peculiar antics of the basketball officials at Saturday night's Heidelberg game, consistent with the quality of refereeing the Bishops have been seeing this season, we became aware that a new kind of sportsmanship has crowded its way into the American scene.

Basketball refs no longer arbitrarily call fouls on individual players; they now suggest two or three possibilities picked at random from both teams and then arbitrarily decide on who fouled.

In radio, television and movies, examples of this new look in sportsmanship are also evident. One popular record, heard constantly on the radio, dramatically describes a teenager's valiant attempt to rescue his true love. She, the story goes, is fishing for his high-school ring lost in the car (which is stalled on the railroad track.) Despite her noble gamble, this contrived lyric is resolved when the train roars through, making a teen-angel out of her.

A sporty try, but she loses.

But heroic sportsmanship does pay off for T.V.'s "untouchables," Eliot Ness and Jack Paar. The former, though on every week for an hour, is sure never to capture the same crooks twice. The latter, on the air five nights a week, had his ups by trying to tell a sporty joke that ended with his Downs.

And the "silver screen," which has given us many characters of outstanding conduct such as Frankenstein, Dracula and King Kong, has added a new version of Jack The Ripper (which should be more appropriately titled "Son of Jack the Ripper"). It is Jack, a practicing surgeon by day and field worker by night, who engages his victims in a moment of pleasant conversation when they first meet, thus allowing them a sporting chance.

But, finding that women can't stomach him, Jack applies his gay blade, and has a ripping good time doing it, too.

This unique departure in sportsmanship will be seen on the Ohio Wesleyan campus next fall. For then Red Paint is to replace the Sulphur Spring as the dink penalty.

The freshman noses, the paint and the brushes will probably all be provided by an appropriate committee - the test of sportsmanship will be in seeing whether the sophomores give a tinker's dam.

The Ohio Wesleyan grapplers dropped their sixth match of the season to Hiram at Edwards Gymnasium last Saturday.

Last Wednesday they were decisioned by Wabash, 22-6.

In the 19-8 loss to Hiram, Bert Laub presented the most thrilling match when he fought his opponent to a 2-2 draw.

Leo Matthews won his match, 4-2, in the 147 lb. class, and George Menges defeated his man in a close decision at 167 lbs.

Against Wabash, Menges and Chris Hetzel were the only two victors for the Bishops. Menges wrestled to a 10-8 win, and Hetzel, experiencing his first varsity match, dumped his opponent, 8-2, in the heavyweight division.

The team suffered a further loss against Hiram when Lew Jones sustained an arm injury which will probably keep him out of action for the remainder of the season.

articles.headline: Gutknecht Runs Best
articles.body:
Ex-OWU runner John Gutknecht is competing for the Baltimore Olympic Club. Currently studying zoology at the University of North Carolina, Gutknecht has found time to compete in several meets.

He turned in his best personal time in the two-mile run, placing fourth in the Philadelphia Inquirer Games with a time of 9 min. 16 sec. Besides competing in other Eastern indoor meets, Gutknecht finished 13th in the National AAU 10,000 meter run.

articles.headline: Robin Farran Athlete of the Week
articles.body:
Robin Farran has been selected Athlete of the Week for the first time in his career on the basis of his command performance against Oberlin last Saturday.

Entered by Coach Gordin in the 200-yd. breast stroke, Farran surprised everyone by nosing out his own teammate, Jerry Dickey, and swimming to first place in the event.

In doing so, he set a new OWU mark of 2:39.1. This eclipses the old standard of 2:41.8 set this year by Dickey.

Earlier in the meet Farran picked up another blue ribbon in the 200-yd. individual medley with the winning time of 2:30.5.

The slightly built sophomore has improved this season and according to Gordin "will be heavily counted on in the conference meet."
